KEY MESSAGE 1...
The coastal low pressure system southeast of the Delmarva 
Region this afternoon will track northeast towards southeast New
England and Cape Cod tonight. This track is much further east 
than the past few days. The high-resolution CAMS, global and 
ensembles guidance is all showing this passage of the low 
further east. A sharp gradient exists with the wave being so far
east and being progressive. PoPs were lowered into the slight 
chance to high chance range (20-50%) from the mid Hudson Valley,
Taconics into western New England for much lighter rainfall 
amounts with the fast moving wave. Rainfall totals will only 
amount from a few hundredths to a tenth of an inch, though 
portions of Litchfield County, CT may receive a tenth to a 
quarter of an inch on the northwest side of the fast moving wave
associated with its mid and upper deformation zone. Locations 
from the Capital Region, Lake George Region and the eastern 
Catskills north and west will stay mainly rain free outside a 
few sprinkles. It will be a mild tonight compared to the past 
several with clouds around, as the cold front will remain to the
west of the region associated with the northern stream trough 
approaching. Lows based on the NBM will be in the 40s to lower 
50s. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A strong cold front moves across the region in the afternoon
into the early evening. A few light showers associated with the
cold front may impact the western Adirondacks, southern Greens
and northern Catskills. The strong cold advection, channeled
flow, some momentum transfer from 2-3 kft AGL and deeper mixing
may allow for some wind gusts in the 25-35 mph range in the 
Mohawk Valley, Greater Capital Region, northern Catskills, 
northern Taconics and the Berkshires. A few isolated gusts 35-40
mph can not be ruled out. Max temps may peak in the late 
morning to early pm. Highs will be in the upper 40s to lower/mid
50s over the higher terrain and mid 50s to lower 60s in the 
valleys (a few mid 60s in the mid Hudson Valley).

In the post-frontal cold advection, H850 temps tumble 
to -8C to -12C Mon night into Tue morning across eastern NY and
western New England. As the boundary layer flow veers from the 
west/northwest to northwest, some lake effect snow showers may 
impact the western Mohawk Valley, and the northern and eastern 
Catskills. Slight/low chance PoPs were added to the forecast 
based on the latest CAMS. Any snow accumulation will be light, 
as a coating to a tenth of an inch may occur. Lows fall into 
the 20s to lower 30s.

KEY MESSAGE 3...
A trend to tranquil and dry weather for Tuesday into the busy
travel day on Wednesday. The mid-level trough axis moves through
on Tuesday with some brisk conditions still. Any lake effect
will end in the morning with the flow becoming north/northwest
and the subsidence inversion lowering. Temps trend colder than
normal by 5 degrees or so with 30s and lower 40s and some upper
30s over the northern mtns. High pressure builds in with
diminishing winds Tue night into Wed with cold conditions. 

Majority of the ensembles, medium-range deterministic guidance,
and ensembles keep Wed night dry, as a broad mid and upper level
trough sets up over the eastern CONUS. The trough becomes
negatively tilted Thu morning, as a double-barrel low pressure
system or a coastal low moves toward the Northeast. A deep fetch
or Atlantic and Gulf moisture will occur, as PWATS rise above
normal. Low-level H850 u-component wind anomalies /easterlies/ 
increase several deviations above normal tapping into the 
moisture, also the threat of strong gusty winds will likely 
increase off the western New England higher terrain 
Thanksgiving/Thanksgiving night, as the latest 24-hr NBM probs 
for max wind gusts >40 mph ending 06Z/1 am Fri are 40-60% for 
the southern Taconics, southern Greens, Berkshires and 
Litchfield Hills. 

The challenge continue to be the track of the system and the
pcpn types. The air mass will be dry and cold ahead of the
system. The sfc high moves well downstream, so the sub-freezing
cold air will have trouble remaining in place, though some snow
or a wintry mix may occur over the higher elevations due to wet
bulb cooling. A brief mix (wet bulb cooling) may also occur in 
the valleys, but a transition to rainfall will likely occur. If 
the pcpn starts later in the day, then warmer profiles may 
occur. Much of the guidance does show a transition to rainfall 
with a low pressure system along or near the coast Thursday 
afternoon into the evening, but some uncertainty continues to 
exist. The 24-hour Winter Storm Severity Index Probabilistic 
(WSSI-P)guidance ending 7 AM Friday indicates 20-30% probs for 
minor impacts across higher terrain areas, and 5-10% for valley 
areas from the Capital Region north and west, suggesting some 
winter travel conditions are possible Thu/Thu night mainly
